qs.q: An obstetrician counsels parents about a prenatal diagnosis of trisomy 18 (Edward syndrome). How does the general prognosis of Edward syndrome compare to Down syndrome?
o: Edward syndrome has a mild phenotype with normal adult survival, while Down syndrome is uniformly fatal in the neonatal period
Both trisomies present with identical life expectancies and equally mild developmental phenotypes
Severe malformations give Edward syndrome a life expectancy usually under one year, whereas Down syndrome is milder with survival to 50-60 years
Trisomy 18 is classified as a structural rearrangement rather than an autosomal trisomy
qs.e: Edward syndrome and Patau syndrome involve severe malformations with life expectancy typically under one year, whereas Down syndrome presents a milder phenotype allowing survival to 50 to 60 years.

qs.q: When is prenatal diagnosis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically possible using chorionic villus sampling?
qs.e: Prenatal diagnosis is possible late in the first trimester by chorionic villus sampling or during the second trimester by amniocentesis. Amniocentesis is reserved for the second trimester rather than the first.

qs.q: A clinical genetics team discusses screening and diagnostic modalities for congenital anomalies. Which of the following combinations consists entirely of invasive methods of prenatal diagnosis?
o: Chorionic villous sampling with percutaneous cordocentesis
Obstetric ultrasound with chorionic villous sampling
qs.e: Chorionic villous sampling (CVS) and percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (cordocentesis) are invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures. Obstetric ultrasound and MRI are non-invasive imaging modalities.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Prenatal diagnosis identifies fetal genetic or structural abnormalities before birth, guiding management and parental choices. Techniques include CVS, amniocentesis, and non‑invasive testing.

sections.p: Prenatal diagnosis refers to any test performed during pregnancy to detect fetal anomalies, ranging from chromosomal disorders to single‑gene mutations and structural defects.
b: Invasive: chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 10‑13 weeks, amniocentesis at 15‑20 weeks.
Non‑invasive: cell‑free fetal DNA (cffDNA) in maternal blood after 10 weeks.

t.b: What chromosomal or single‑gene abnormality does it detect? → Direct karyotype, FISH, PCR for specific mutations.
What structural or genetic information is obtained? → Karyotype, microarray, targeted gene panels.
What common trisomies can be screened? → Trisomy 21, 18, 13; high sensitivity but not diagnostic.

sections.p: Abnormalities are graded by established systems (e.g., ISUOG for structural defects, ACMG for genetic variants) to guide counseling and intervention.
b: Mild: isolated, treatable lesions (e.g., small ventricular septal defect).
Moderate: multisystem involvement, possible post‑natal surgery (e.g., spina bifida).
Severe: lethal or life‑limiting (e.g., anencephaly, trisomy 13).

sections.p: Most prenatal abnormalities arise from genetic errors, but maternal infections and environmental exposures also contribute, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Chromosomal nondisjunction (trisomy 21, 18, 13).
Single‑gene mutations (e.g., cystic fibrosis, sickle cell).
Maternal infections: TORCH (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis), malaria, HIV‑related placental insufficiency.
Environmental toxins: aflatoxin, herbal teratogens.

sections.p: Fetal abnormalities are often silent to the mother; clues arise from abnormal ultrasound findings, abnormal serum markers, or positive cffDNA screens.
b: Nuchal translucency >3.5 mm suggests chromosomal abnormality.
Elevated AFP indicates neural tube defect or abdominal wall defect.
Absent cardiac activity on Doppler signals fetal demise.

sections.p: A stepwise approach uses screening first, then diagnostic testing if risk is high.

t.b: What risk does it estimate? → Probability of trisomy 21/18; high risk prompts CVS.
What structural abnormality does it reveal? → Detects cardiac, CNS, skeletal defects; guides targeted testing.
What condition does a markedly high level suggest? → Open neural tube defect; confirm with detailed ultrasound.
What common trisomies are screened? → 21, 18, 13; a positive result requires invasive confirmation.

sections.p: Certain findings demand urgent referral to a fetal medicine unit.
b: Severe hydrocephalus with rapid head growth.
Persistent severe oligohydramnios.
Fetal anemia (elevated MCA Doppler) in maternal malaria or sickle cell disease.

sections.p: Management balances treating the underlying cause, preparing for delivery, and supporting parental decision‑making.
b: Genetic counseling for confirmed chromosomal or single‑gene disorders.
Intra‑uterine therapy: fetal blood transfusion for anemia, laser ablation for twin‑twin transfusion.
Maternal treatment of infections (e.g., antimalarials, antiretrovirals) to reduce fetal harm.
Avoid teratogenic drugs; use folic acid supplementation to prevent neural‑tube defects.

sections.p: After a diagnosis, schedule serial ultrasounds, consider fetal MRI, and plan delivery at a tertiary center if needed.
b: Vaccination against rubella, screening for HIV/TB, and malaria prophylaxis in endemic areas.
Family planning and pre‑implantation genetic testing for recurrent disorders.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic prenatal findings can lead to misdiagnosis.
b: Physiologic polyhydramnios vs. gastrointestinal obstruction.
Transient ventriculomegaly vs. true hydrocephalus.
Maternal obesity obscuring ultrasound detection of defects.

sections.p: Some tests have limitations that may produce false‑positive or false‑negative results.
b: cffDNA cannot detect balanced translocations or single‑gene disorders.
Elevated AFP can be due to multiple gestation or fetal demise, not only neural‑tube defects.
Low PAPP‑A may be seen in maternal hypertension, not just chromosomal abnormality.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly increasing fetal head circumference suggesting hydrocephalus
Severe oligohydramnios with fetal growth restriction
Maternal fever with rash in the first trimester (possible TORCH infection)

faq.q: Is a normal ultrasound enough to rule out genetic disease?
faq.a: No; structural scans miss many chromosomal or single‑gene disorders, which require genetic testing.

faq.q: Can prenatal diagnosis be done without risk to the fetus?
faq.a: Non‑invasive tests (cffDNA) carry no fetal risk, but definitive diagnosis usually needs invasive sampling with a small miscarriage risk.

faq.q: What if the required test is unavailable locally?
faq.a: Arrange referral to a regional center or use the nearest available screening method and counsel based on risk.
